sec.title: Background
sec.p: We aimed to develop an actionable and feasible prospective clinical model to estimate toxicity risk to assist chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy providers with the management of patients with relapsed and/or refractory large B-cell lymphoma.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We conducted an observational, retrospective cohort study using secondary data from 390 patients treated with the CD19 CAR T-cell therapy axicabtagene ciloleucel under two prospective clinical trials, ZUMA-1 and ZUMA-7; these clinical trials enrolled patients with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma between 2015 and 2019. Using machine learning and statistical methods, we developed a classification model for identifying patients unlikely to experience early cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurological events (NE) of any grade.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We found the use of prophylactic corticosteroids to be an important factor in remaining CRS-free and NE-free within the first 3 days post-treatment (p<0.001). We identified a top model for no early CRS/NE using a set of six pre-lymphodepletion clinicopathologic features: number of lines of prior systemic therapy, age, baseline tumor burden (as measured by sum of the product of the diameters), C-reactive protein, aspartate transaminase, and hemoglobin, which achieves a positive predictive value of 0.71 in the holdout validation cohort. Additionally, we find that predicted probabilities generated from the model are strongly associated with incidence of Grade 2 or higher NE.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: We illustrated that routine clinicopathologic variables can be used to identify patients at low risk of developing early post-treatment CRS and/or NE. Such knowledge can be used to help treating centers prospectively manage patient care, including consideration of outpatient treatment.
Keywords: Chimeric antigen receptor - CAR, Cytokine release syndrome, Lymphoma, Neurotoxicity, T cell
Received 2025 Mar 13; Accepted 2025 Jul 11; Collection date 2025.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy experts suggested that validated predictive models to assess toxicity risk are needed to help select chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy patients who are more amenable to outpatient monitoring compared with those who may be at higher risk for toxicity and warrant closer monitoring.

This research applies a robust statistical methodology to clinical trial data from 390 patients with large B-cell lymphoma treated with axicabtagene ciloleucel to develop a model to predict no early cytokine release syndrome (CRS) or neurotoxicity (NE) using routine clinicopathological markers collected on/before lymphodepletion.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: Our model achieves a positive predictive value >0.70 in a holdout validation cohort of nearly 80 patients, suggesting that standard, readily-available clinical markers can identify, at least 5 days prior to infusion, those patients who are unlikely to experience early CRS/NE. This information could support outpatient administration and monitoring strategies in low-risk patients, or through the intensification of monitoring and early interventions in high-risk patients, which may result in more efficient healthcare delivery and improved patient outcomes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The first autologous anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy product axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) approved for use in large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) has shown remarkable efficacy in both clinical trials and the real-world setting1,4; however, toxicities associated with this class of therapy, that is, cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic events (NE), are common and can require patient hospitalization.5 In the pivotal ZUMA-1 and ZUMA-7 clinical trials, more than 90% and 60% of patients experienced CRS and/or NE of any grade, with median time to onset of 2–3 days and 5–7 days, respectively.2 3 Preliminary results of the ZUMA-24 clinical trial, which evaluated axi-cel toxicity outcomes in patients with relapse/refractory (R/R) LBCL treated and monitored in the outpatient setting after receiving prophylactic corticosteroids for three consecutive days starting on the infusion day, found the median time to hospitalization to be 4 days.6

With the rapid development of CAR-T cell therapy adverse event management protocols, including development of prophylactic or earlier intervention approaches to improve safety outcomes without impacting efficacy, there has been increasing community interest in exploring outpatient administration of CAR-T cell therapy. Some authorized treatment centers, although a minority, have made institutional investments to infuse and monitor most CAR-T patients in the outpatient setting.7,10 Not only does outpatient administration of CAR-T cell therapy free up valuable hospital bed space, but it also improves patient experience.7 The American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy recently convened a group of experts in hematology, oncology and cellular therapy to provide a comprehensive review around matters related to CAR-T treatment and monitoring in the outpatient setting.11 Oluwole et al11 suggest that validated predictive models to assess toxicity risk are needed to help select patients who are more amenable to outpatient monitoring compared with those who may be at higher risk for toxicity and warrant closer monitoring.

There have been many attempts to understand and predict post-treatment toxicity outcomes in the broader CAR-T patient population (eg,912,15), although it is important to note that the toxicity outcome definitions, the populations of interest, and the analysis methods differ widely across the numerous studies. The majority of previous investigations using clinicopathologic data were largely focused on elucidating associations between a few selected markers of inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, or disease burden, with high-grade toxicity outcomes. Additionally, although considered a prophylactic intervention rather than a predictive model per se, the use of prophylactic corticosteroids has been observed to delay onset of CRS/NE and is associated with lower rate of high-grade CRS.6 16

Although these results represent a promising direction in post-CAR T biomarker identification, to date, there have been no studies to our knowledge that have investigated the outcome of any grade, early onset CRS/NE toxicity nor that have evaluated the usefulness of pre-lymphodepletion clinicopathologic markers to predict such incidence. As suggested by11 the identification of low- (and/or high-) risk patients prior to the start of lymphodepletion could be instrumental in resource optimization. This could be consequential by enabling outpatient administration and monitoring strategies in low-risk patients, or through the intensification of monitoring and early interventions in high-risk patients, which may result in more efficient healthcare delivery and improved patient outcomes.

In this research, we apply a machine learning training and validation analysis strategy to data collected from axi-cel registrational trials for patients with R/R LBCL. Using data routinely collected in the clinic setting prior to the start of pre-CAR-T lymphodepletion, we develop a top-performing clinicopathologic model to identify CAR-T patients unlikely to experience early post-treatment CRS and/or NE.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This is an observational, retrospective cohort study and represents secondary use of data from two prospective clinical trials: ZUMA-1 (NCT02348216) and ZUMA-7 (NCT03391466).

The primary objective of this secondary data analysis was to identify a generalizable model that uses actionable and feasible pre-lymphodepletion clinicopathologic markers to identify patients with LBCL being treated in the second line or higher (2L+) setting who are at low risk for early, acute CRS and NE following axi-cel treatment.

sec.title: Cohort selection/patient population
sec.p: This study included 390 patients treated with axi-cel under multiple cohorts in the Phase 2 ZUMA-1 clinical trial (NCT02348216; Cohorts 1+2: 217,19; Cohort 3: 20; ZUMA-1 Cohort 4: 17; ZUMA-1 Cohort 6: 21), enrolled between 2015 and 2019, and the ZUMA-7 clinical trial (NCT03391466; 217,19), enrolling between 2018 and 2019. Key protocol criteria across the study cohorts are found in online supplemental table S1. In brief, the full patient cohort included adults with R/R LBCL, diagnosed with diffuse (DLBCL), primary mediastinal, or high-grade LBCL, or transformed follicular lymphoma subtypes. All patients in the full cohort received the standard cyclophosphamide-fludarabine lymphodepletion regimen starting on Day −5 (ie, 5 days prior to the planned CAR T-cell infusion); axi-cel was administered as a single infusion on Day 0 and patients were monitored at a healthcare facility at least daily for a minimum of 7 days following the infusion. As CRS and NE are common adverse events following CAR T-cell therapy, specific guidelines were provided to clinical/investigative study teams related to monitoring and reporting of these events.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Primary data were collected and analyzed by Kite Pharma, a Gilead Company, and its affiliates. Data for this secondary use study were analyzed internally by Kite Pharma, a Gilead Company. Datasets for the clinical trial primary analyses, as specified in the clinical study protocols, were used for this analysis. For patients who may have received axi-cel re-treatment, only data from the patient’s first axi-cel treatment were analyzed.

sec.title: Variable and outcome design
sec.p: The outcome of interest was a binary variable indicating whether the patient experienced any CRS or NE on Days 0, 1, or 2, following axi-cel infusion, where Day 0 was defined as the infusion day. If a patient had no CRS and no NE on Days 0, 1, and 2 post-CAR-T, the variable was coded as “no early CRS/NE toxicity” and as “some early CRS/NE toxicity” otherwise. The positive outcome was considered to be “no early CRS/NE toxicity”. As described in the respective clinical trial protocols, CRS events were graded per Lee criteria22 and neurologic events were graded using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE). Identification of neurological events was previously described in Neelapu et al2 and Locke et al (2022a).3

The candidate markers, all of which were considered to be routinely available in the real-world clinical setting, were collected at baseline (ie, between the clinical trial screening visit and the start of the lymphodepletion regimen on Day −5). Markers included demographics (age, sex, race, ethnicity), baseline disease characteristics (eg, subtype, double/triple hit status, stage, number of prior lines of systemic therapy, baseline tumor burden as measured by sum of the products of two largest perpendicular diameters (SPD)), and routine laboratory markers (eg, albumin, liver enzymes, creatinine, C-reactive protein (CRP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), ferritin, and others). A full list of the more than 50 candidate markers and coding definitions is captured in online supplemental table S2. All laboratory markers were coded with reference to the institutional laboratory normal range and using a standard clinical trials toxicity grading system (ie, CTCAE) using ordinal scales rather than continuous variables—intended both to minimize discrepancies that may arise from differences in laboratory reporting and to ensure that the model can be easily applied in a real-world clinical setting.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: At the outset, the full dataset encompassing the multiple cohorts of ZUMA-1 and the ZUMA-7 clinical trials was randomly split into an 80% development cohort and a 20% holdout validation cohort. Covariate balance of key clinical prognostic features (ie, age, cell of origin, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, International Prognostic Index (IPI), tumor burden (using SPD), and lines of prior therapy) between the development and holdout validation cohorts was evaluated by the failure to detect statistically significant differences across groups using an unadjusted statistical test appropriate to the variable type. Once covariate balance was achieved, the 20% holdout validation cohort was not touched until the final model was selected for independent model validation (figure 1).

caption.title: Methodology used in model development and validation. Data from ZUMA clinical trial patients (ie, ZUMA-1 Phase 2 Cohorts 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6; ZUMA-7) treated with axicabtagene ciloleucel were included in this analysis. Data were split randomly into an 80% development and 20% holdout validation cohort, with covariate balance across age, cell of origin, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG), International Prognostic Index (IPI), tumor burden (using sum of the product of diameters), and lines of prior therapy. Using the top 15 markers identified in feature selection, all unique variable combinations of up to six markers (ie, more than 10,000 unique models) were evaluated using a logistic regression model in the in-bag sample across 100 iterations of random sampling; model performance was summarized in both the in-bag and out-of-bag samples. The performance of the top model was evaluated in the holdout validation cohort.

sec.p: The extent of missing data was evaluated (table 1) and variables with >20% missingness were excluded from consideration as candidate variables in models. For all other covariate missingness, under the assumption of missing at random, a non-parametric, random forest-based missing value imputation method23 was applied first to the development cohort and then to the holdout validation cohort; sensitivity analyses using the set of complete case data were also performed.

sec.p: Feature selection was implemented in the development cohort using univariate analysis, weight of evidence and information value, penalized logistic regression (L1/lasso penalty), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). Cross-validation was used to tune the hyperparameters for these algorithms and iterated over bootstrap resamples and/or different random seeds, as applicable. Variable rankings (rank 1 being the best) were assigned for each method and variable importance across the four feature selection methods was aggregated using truncated enhanced Borda aggregation.24

All models were developed in the development cohort and model performance was assessed using positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Using the top 15 markers identified through feature selection, we conducted an exhaustive search of all combinations of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 markers in a logistic regression model. Within the development cohort, we iteratively selected 75% of patients at random for the in-bag sample, on which the model was trained, and the remaining 25% of patients for the out-of-bag sample (figure 1). This was implemented iteratively for 100 resamples to estimate the variability in performance estimates for each candidate model in both the in-bag and out-of-bag samples (figure 1). To ensure that fewer patients were incorrectly classified as having no early CRS/NE toxicity, the model-specific and resample-specific classification cutpoint was selected to favor specificity over sensitivity using a function to optimize specificity given the minimum constraint on sensitivity of 0.25.25 For each model and performance metric across both the in-bag and out-of-bag samples, the estimated mean and SEM across the 100 resamples were tabulated. Top models were identified as those meeting a minimum threshold of 0.65 for AUROC (indicating that the model was well-performing as a classifier generally) and ranked based on high mean PPV. Noting that PPV depends on the prevalence of the condition, this choice reflects the probability of a clinician making a correct classification for a specific patient being treated, which we deemed most appropriate for ranking model performance.

Sensitivity analyses were performed in the development cohort for all top models prior to validating in the holdout validation cohort. All top models were evaluated in a logistic regression model with adjustment for study/cohort to ensure no discernible differences in model and conclusions using the likelihood ratio test for nested models. Additionally, top models were evaluated with additional adjustment (in separate models) for sex, race, and ethnicity, also using the likelihood ratio test for nested models, to ensure no evident bias or poor model fit across demographic groups. An additional set of sensitivity analyses was run to ensure that six biomarkers were sufficient to capture the best model performance. Finally, using partial dependence plots as a guide, we evaluated whether any of the ordinal variables could be collapsed to fewer categories and still retain similar model performance and conclusions. Assuming independence of observations, final models were evaluated for adherence to model assumptions and model fit, including assessment of multicollinearity, outliers, linearity between covariates and the logit of the outcome, model calibration, and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test.

The top-performing final model was selected for independent validation in the holdout validation cohort. For the final model, the model coefficients and the classification cutpoint were defined on the full development cohort. The final development model was then applied to the 20% holdout validation cohort and model performance, including the confusion matrix, PPV, sensitivity, and specificity, was summarized for both the development and holdout validation cohorts. Distributions of variables in the final model were visualized using stratified boxplots or stacked bar plots and relative variable importance was determined using the absolute value of the t-statistic for each variable in the multivariable model.

Post hoc analyses were also conducted to evaluate the association between other toxicity outcomes (eg, high grade CRS and NE) and the final model using both the dichotomous classification (ie, using Fisher’s exact or χ2 test, as appropriate), as well as the final model predicted probabilities (using both Wilcoxon rank-sum test and two-sample t-test). (Note that our model considers no early CRS/NE toxicity as the positive outcome whereby high-grade CRS and NE toxicity were considered the positive outcomes for this post hoc analysis, thus changing the expected directionality of the predicted probabilities.)

Although evaluation of statistical association was not the primary objective of this research, when applicable in ancillary analyses, a two-sided alpha level of 0.05 was used to identify statistical significance, using no adjustments for multiplicity.

Analysis dataset programming was conducted in SAS (V.9.4). Statistical analyses were conducted in R (R V.4.1.0) with packages dplyr (V.1.1.2), tidyr (V.1.3.0), ggplot2 (V.3.4.4), ggpubr (V.0.6.0), cutpointr (V.1.1.2), base (V.4.1.0), caret (V.6.0–89), and corrplot (V.0.90).

sec.title: Patient characteristics and toxicity outcomes
sec.p: Demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients enrolled and treated under the ZUMA-1 and ZUMA-7 clinical trial protocols have been previously reported (ZUMA-1 NCT02348216; Cohorts 1+2: 217,19; Cohort 3: 20; ZUMA-1 Cohort 4: 17; ZUMA-1 Cohort 6: 21; ZUMA-7: 3). In brief, the median age in the development cohort was 59 years old (IQR: 15 years). The majority were male (63%), Caucasian (83%), and of non-Hispanic ethnicity (92%). Most patients presented with stage III/IV disease (77%), no bone marrow involvement (90%), a baseline ECOG score of 1 (52%), standard IPI score of 0–2 (53%), and refractory to the last line of therapy (83%). The median baseline tumor burden as measured at the screening visit using CT or positron emission tomography was 2,794 mm2 (IQR: 4,768 mm2) (table 1). Data missingness was high for clinical ferritin (49%) and molecular subtype (36%); as a result, these variables were excluded from modeling analyses. Post hoc analysis demonstrated similar patient characteristics in the holdout validation cohort (online supplemental table S3). Additionally, an examination of pairwise Spearman correlations across variables in the development cohort demonstrated a low degree of correlation generally, indicated by absolute estimated correlation coefficients <0.20, with higher correlations observed among related variables, including IPI and IPI components, disease type variables, and others (online supplemental figure S1).

106 patients (38%) in the development cohort experienced no early CRS/NE toxicity (table 2, online supplemental table S3). This percentage was similar for patients in the holdout validation cohort (ie, 41%) (table 2, online supplemental table S3). Post hoc analysis of elevated toxicity outcomes demonstrates that, across the full dataset, 139 (40%) patients experienced Grade 2 or higher NE while 90 (26%) patients experienced Grade 3 or higher neurotoxicity (online supplemental table S3). Grade 2+ and Grade 3+CRS was observed in the full cohort for 191 patients (55%) and 24 patients (7%), respectively (online supplemental table S3).

sec.title: Use of prophylactic corticosteroids may be an important factor in remaining CRS-free and NE-free on Days 0–2 post-CAR T-cell therapy
sec.p: In our analysis, ZUMA-1 Cohort 6 membership (yes vs no) was found to be a principal factor in identifying no early CRS/NE toxicity (p<0.0001). This finding was identified through a planned sensitivity analysis in which top candidate models were evaluated to ensure that study and study cohort did not significantly improve the final model. No concerns with any other study/cohort were noted. As observed in the tabulation of key differences across study and cohort (online supplemental table S1), one distinguishing feature in ZUMA-1 Cohort 6 was the prophylactic administration of pretreatment corticosteroids (specifically, 10 mg dexamethasone) on Days 0–2. Although there were some observed differences in pretreatment features between ZUMA-1 Cohort 6 and other study/cohorts (online supplemental table S4), there was no definitive trend in the directionality of these prognostic features. For example, although ZUMA-1 Cohort 6 patients had lower baseline tumor burden on average, they were also more likely to be older, have more lines of prior therapy on average, and were more likely to be classified as triple hit (online supplemental table S4). Consequent to this finding, and because prophylactic corticosteroid use reflects a management strategy rather than a baseline characteristic per se, we excluded patients from ZUMA-1 Cohort 6 from further analyses to identify a prognostic model for identifying patients without early CRS/NE toxicity.

sec.title: Multivariable feature selection and modeling identify top pre-lymphodepletion variables for association with no early CRS/NE toxicity
sec.p: Aggregated variable importance rankings (online supplemental figure S2) identified number of lines of prior therapy to be a key feature in identifying whether a patient will or will not experience early CRS or NE toxicity. Refractory status to the last line of anti-LBCL therapy, as well as baseline tumor burden (as measured by SPD) and baseline ferritin, were also shown in this patient cohort to be key factors in understanding early post-infusion toxicity. Additionally, hemoglobin (independent of transfusion) and clinical CRP values prior to lymphodepletion were also key determinants (online supplemental figure S2).

Identification of top-performing models selected older age and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), in addition to number of lines of prior therapy, baseline tumor burden, hemoglobin, and clinical CRP. The distributions of these variables in the development cohort, as well as their variable importance value and ranking, are seen in figure 2A–F,G, respectively. Notably, in a multivariable model, number of prior lines of therapy has the largest variable importance, with fewer lines of therapy associated with no early CRS/NE toxicity, followed by younger age (<65 years). The only variable exhibiting a positive association with no early CRS/NE toxicity was hemoglobin at lymphodepletion—indicating that patients with values above the institutional, gender-specific lower limit of normal were more likely to have no early CRS/NE toxicity (figure 2C,G).

sec.title: Pre-lymphodepletion clinicopathologic covariates alone reliably identify patients with no early CRS/NE toxicity
sec.p: The final model included the following pre-lymphodepletion variables: baseline tumor burden as measured by SPD, clinical CRP, hemoglobin at Day −5, number of lines of prior therapy, age, and AST at Day −5. Model detail, including variable coding, model coefficients, and classification cutpoint, is described in online supplemental figure S3. Performance estimates demonstrate that PPV, specificity, sensitivity, and NPV were higher in the development cohort compared with the holdout validation cohort (table 2), which was expected as data from the development cohort were used for model development. In the development cohort, our final model achieved a PPV of 0.84, correctly identifying 27/32 patients to have no early CRS/NE toxicity. Performance in the holdout validation cohort was also robust, achieving a PPV of 0.71 (table 2). Sensitivity in this cohort was slightly lower than in our development cohort, with a sensitivity of 0.17 compared with 0.25. In the development cohort, our top model identified about 12% (32/277) of patients as having no early CRS/NE toxicity and made fewer than 2% errors (5/277) (table 2). In the holdout validation cohort, our model identified about 10% (7/73) as having no early CRS/NE toxicity and made fewer than 3% errors (2/73) (table 2).

sec.title: Patients identified to have no early CRS/NE toxicity were unlikely to experience Grade 3+ CRS or NE within 7 days post-infusion
sec.p: A total of 39 patients across the development and holdout validation cohorts were predicted to have no early CRS/NE toxicity by Day 3. Of these 39 patients, 32 were correctly identified to have no early CRS/NE toxicity, while 7 were incorrect predictions (table 2). For the 32 patients (ie, 27 patients in the development cohort and 5 patients in the holdout validation cohort, table 2) correctly predicted to have no early CRS/NE toxicity by Day 3, 1 patient experienced Grade 3 CRS following Day 3, 13 patients developed a maximum of Grade 2 CRS, and 4 patients developed Grade 2 NE between Day 3 and 7 (figure 3A,B).

caption.title: CRS and NE toxicity experience for patients correctly and incorrectly classified as no early CRS/NE toxicity. The frequency of patients with cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and/or neurologic toxicity (NE) on Days 0–7 post-treatment by maximum grade is presented for (A) patients in the development cohort who were correctly classified as having no early CRS/NE toxicity (n=27); (B) patients in the holdout validation cohort who were correctly classified as having no early CRS/NE toxicity (n=5); (C) patients in the development cohort who were incorrectly classified as having no early CRS/NE toxicity (n=5); and (D) patients in the validation cohort who were incorrectly classified as having no early CRS/NE toxicity (n=2). Notably, patients correctly classified as having no early CRS/NE toxicity had no CRS/NE toxicity until on/after Day 3 whereas those patient incorrectly classified as having no early CRS/NE toxicity did have some CRS/NE toxicity on Days 0–2.

sec.p: Seven patients were incorrectly identified as having no early CRS/NE toxicity (ie, five patients in the development cohort and two patients in the holdout validation cohort, table 2). Of these seven, all experienced CRS within Days 0–2 post-CAR-T; one patient experienced Grade 2 CRS on Day 1 and the other six patients experienced Grade 1 CRS within this same period (figure 3C,D). None of these seven patients experienced NE of any grade within Days 0–2 post-CAR-T (figure 3C,D). When looking at the toxicity trajectory for these seven patients over the first 7 days post-CAR-T (inclusive), three patients had a maximum of Grade 2 CRS and one patient experienced Grade 3 NE (figure 3C,D).

The baseline profile of these seven misclassified patients was also of interest. All of these seven patients had one prior line of therapy, were younger than 65 years, had CRP and AST values lower than the upper limit of normal, and tumor burden as measured by SPD lower than the median value—and most were lower than the first quartile. Four of these patients had hemoglobin above the lower limit of normal, and three of these patients had lower baseline hemoglobin. Although not a variable contained within the final model, all seven patients also had imputed clinical ferritin values below the median—and most values were lower than the first quartile. Thus, these patients had few notable risk factors but nonetheless experienced an early CRS/NE event.

sec.title: Prediction based on pre-lymphodepletion clinicopathologic covariates also associate with incidence of high-grade CRS or NE toxicity
sec.p: We evaluated the associations between our final model predictions and other toxicity outcomes, including incidence of Grade 2 or higher and Grade 3 or higher CRS and NE toxicity experienced at any time post-infusion, as previously described. We observed a statistically significant association between the predicted probabilities from our final model and the incidence of Grade 2 or higher and Grade 3 or higher NE toxicity (both p<0.0001, figure 4). Specifically, on average, patients with higher predicted probabilities of no early CRS/NE toxicity were less likely than their counterparts to develop Grade 2 or higher NE; that is, patients with a lower predicted probability of having no early CRS/NE toxicity had a higher odds of experiencing Grade 2 or higher NE (OR 1.32 corresponding to a 0.1 decrease in the predicted probability of having no early CRS/NE toxicity). When evaluating the association between our dichotomous model classifications for no early CRS/NE toxicity and higher-grade NE, we observed a statistically significant association with the incidence of Grade 3+NE (p=0.02) and a trend toward univariate significance also for Grade 2+NE (p=0.08). For the outcomes of Grade 2+CRS and Grade 3+CRS, we did not observe any association—neither with the predicted probabilities nor the dichotomous classification—between our no early CRS/NE toxicity model and these higher-grade CRS outcomes.

caption.title: Distribution of predicted probabilities from no early CRS/NE toxicity model by incidence of Grade 2 or higher neurotoxicity. Boxplots of the distributions of predicted probabilities stratified by higher grade toxicity outcome are provided. Predicted probabilities are higher on average for patients with no Grade 2+NE (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve: 0.64) (A) and also with no Grade 3+NE (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve: 0.65) (B), suggesting that our model for no early CRS/NE toxicity also has some strength in identifying patients without higher grade NE toxicity, noting that the no early CRS/NE toxicity outcome is correlated with other toxicity outcomes. CRS, cytokine release syndrome; NE, neurotoxicity.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Actionable and feasible clinicopathologic variables alone, collected on or before the start of lymphodepletion, can be used to identify patients who are unlikely to experience early CRS/NE toxicity post-CAR-T, with a PPV exceeding 0.70 in an independent hold-out validation cohort of 73 patients. The number of prior lines of therapy, baseline tumor burden as measured by SPD, and CRP are important variables in identifying patients unlikely to experience early post-CAR-T toxicity. Tumor burden and CRP have been published previously as a tool to identify toxicity.9 12 14 In conjunction, we found that AST and hemoglobin within institutionally defined normal limits may also be used to identify patients with low risk of early toxicity; these may demonstrate mechanistic findings that would need to be validated experimentally or indicate another dysfunction. Low hemoglobin is indicative of anemia, which is frequent in patients with cancer and can be caused by several factors, including chronic inflammation which inhibits erythropoiesis and decreases bone marrow capacity due to administration of multiple lines of chemotherapy and radiation therapy as well as bone marrow involvement.26 Other strategies used comorbidities, for example, liver or kidney impairment, as criteria for not placing patients in the outpatient setting for CAR-T9 (Dholaria et al). Furthermore, these factors have been described as prognostic biomarkers of poor outcome in DLBCL. In a study examining patients with DLBCL treated with standard first-line chemotherapy regimens, elevated pretreatment AST levels associated with many unfavorable clinical characteristics, which included elevated LDH level, high-risk IPI (IPI 3–5), non-germinal center B-cell subtypes, and more extranodal involvement.27 Similar evaluation of baseline levels of hemoglobin/anemia in DLBCL has found this factor to be significantly associated with older age (ie, 60 years or older), extranodal sites (ie, two or more), Ann Arbor stage III or IV, and elevated LDH levels.28

The use of prophylactic corticosteroids may be an important factor in determining whether a patient will remain CRS and NE-free within the first 3 days post-CAR-T. This finding is consistent with the results of ZUMA-1 Cohort 621 and, more recently, preliminary results from the ZUMA-24 clinical trial6 that evaluated incidence and severity of CRS and NE in axi-cel patients treated and monitored in the outpatient setting. While we ultimately decided to exclude ZUMA-1 Cohort 6 patients from our analysis cohort because prophylactic corticosteroid use represents a management intervention rather than a baseline characteristic per se, it is an important finding generally.

Two important aspects should be considered when developing a pretreatment model to help clinicians identify patients who are unlikely to experience early CRS and NE toxicity. First, a decision by clinicians about tolerated risk must be made. In our analysis, we selected a classification cutpoint that prioritized specificity over sensitivity in order to make fewer false positive errors. But this assumption can be changed based on clinician/institution risk tolerance and a different classification cutpoint can be chosen, depending on the institution’s infrastructure and experience treating and managing CAR T-cell therapy patients in their institution. Second, our analysis sought to define a classification model for no early CRS/NE toxicity. In post hoc analyses, we determined that the use of continuous predicted probabilities as a model output could also be beneficial to the community. For example, instead of a dichotomous output defining “no” versus “yes” toxicity, the predicted probability (rather than the dichotomous classification) could be used as a model output to help clinicians understand early CRS/NE toxicity risk, and the determination of a classification cut point could be made on an institution-specific basis.

sec.title: Future directions and limitations
sec.p: This analysis uses data from patients collected in the clinical trial setting. Although the data are thorough and collected uniformly, the patients may not be representative of patients with R/R LBCL treated in the real world; this is a secondary analysis, using data collected between 2015 and 2019 for another purpose and not specifically to answer this research question. Due to the small proportion of patients in our cohort from black and Asian racial groups (<5%), patients from non-white racial groups were considered as a single category. Although sensitivity analyses on the final models were run to evaluate any lack of model fit by race and ethnicity, future model development should include more data from patients of diverse racial and ethnic groups.

Finally, there are many factors that need to be considered in determining whether a CAR-T patient can be treated in the outpatient setting. Many of these factors have been included in this model, while many others have not (eg, comorbidity score and social support). Among routinely collected clinicopathologic markers, ferritin was not collected in the early ZUMA-1 cohorts and was excluded as a candidate for top models due to variable missingness (depicted in table 1). Post hoc multivariable models that incorporated a continuous clinical ferritin value imputed using research-grade pharmacodynamic ferritin measurements, however, demonstrated similar performance to our final model, suggesting that ferritin may indeed be useful but is not mandatory for identifying patients with no early CRS/NE toxicity. This suggests that, whereas ferritin is an important variable in understanding post-treatment CRS/NE, there are other variables—or variable combinations—that can similarly explain patients’ post-treatment CRS/NE experience. Disease subtype (eg, activated B-cell like or germinal center B-cell-like) was also missing for many patients and this variable was also excluded from model consideration. Additionally, definitions used to capture double-hit and triple-hit status changed between initial enrollment of ZUMA-1 Cohort 1 and ZUMA-7; an attempt was made with existing data to make these definitions consistent, but we were unable to ascertain the true effect of these variables (if any) for use in identifying patients with no early CRS/NE toxicity. Due to the above, this should not be interpreted as a one-size-fits-all model for identifying patients with no early CRS/NE toxicity. It should, of course, be used in conjunction with clinical discretion and center-specific infrastructure to ensure patient safety is maintained.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: We have developed a well-performing model using actionable and feasible pre-lymphodepletion clinicopathologic markers to identify patients unlikely to experience early CRS/NE toxicity following axi-cel treatment. These models were developed and validated using a robust methodology with a reasonable sample size and low degree of variable missingness, and findings were supported by sensitivity analyses and model diagnostics. Additionally, all variables in these models are routinely collected in the clinic setting, are defined using the institutional laboratory reference ranges, and are coded using a standard clinical trials toxicity grading system. The final model is interpretable, reasonably simple, understandable to clinicians, accessible to nurse practitioners, and supported by statistics.
